```{r analysis}
# ---- Analysis: every estimate reported in the text is computed here ----
has <- function(d, v) v %in% names(d) && !all(is.na(d[[v]]))

A <- pd[age >= 20 & age <= 59 & sex %in% c("Men", "Women")]
A[, `:=`(sex = droplevels(sex),
         regular = as.integer(pas_group == "Regular wage/salaried"),
         unpaid = unpaid_domestic + unpaid_care,
         any_unpaid = as.integer(unpaid_domestic + unpaid_care > 0),
         no_work = as.integer(employment == 0),
         dom_misc = dom_petcare + dom_travel + dom_other,
         care_adult = care_dep_adult + care_nondep_adult + care_other,
         school_kid = as.integer(hh_n_6_14 > 0))]
if (has(A, "edu_tier")) A[, `:=`(graduate = as.integer(edu_tier == "Graduate and above"),
                                  low_edu = as.integer(edu_tier == "Not literate / below primary"))]
# Roster-based SES proxies (the 2024 person file has no consumption, caste or religion)
if (has(A, "head_edu_tier")) A[, head_grad := as.integer(head_edu_tier == "Graduate and above")]
if (has(A, "hh_max_edu_tier")) A[, hh_max_grad := as.integer(hh_max_edu_tier == "Graduate and above")]
A[, never_married := as.integer(marital == CODE$marital["never_married"])]
# Type of day (1 normal, 2 other): not pre-determined, used only as a robustness restriction
if (has(A, "type_day")) A[, other_day := as.integer(type_day != CODE$type_of_day["normal"])]
# District x sub-round cells for the balance tests
has_dsr <- has(A, "dist_id") && has(A, "sub_round")
if (has_dsr) A[, dist_sr := paste(dist_id, sub_round, sep = "_")]
A[, wife_emp := fifelse(female == 0, as.numeric(spouse_employed), NA_real_)]
A[, mgrp := fcase(female == 0 & pas_group == "Regular wage/salaried", "Regular salaried",
                  female == 0 & pas_group == "Casual labour", "Casual labour",
                  female == 0 & pas_group == "Self-employed", "Self-employed",
                  female == 0 & pas_group == "Student", "Students",
                  female == 0 & pas_group %in% c("Unemployed", "Domestic duties", "Other not working"),
                  "Not in paid work", default = NA_character_)]
A[, `:=`(sun_reg = sunday * regular, sat_reg = saturday * regular)]

# ---- Specification ----
SES_V <- c("i(head_edu_tier)", "i(hh_max_edu_tier)", "hh_any_regular", "hh_n_employed")
CV <- c("i(age_band)", "i(edu_tier)", "married", "urban",
        "hh_size", "hh_n_under6", "hh_n_6_14", "hh_n_60plus", SES_V)
FE_V <- c("dist_id", "sub_round")      # fe() falls back to state if dist_id is absent
cfor <- function(d) ctrl(d, CV)
fes  <- function(d) fe(d, FE_V)
fe_used <- c(if (has(A, "dist_id")) "dist_id" else "state",
             if (has(A, "sub_round") && uniqueN(na.omit(A$sub_round)) > 1) "sub_round")
has_sr <- "sub_round" %in% fe_used
fe_txt <- paste0(if (fe_used[1] == "dist_id") "district" else "state", iff(has_sr, " and survey sub-round (quarter)", ""))

rf <- function(y, d, rhs = cfor(d), f = fes(d)) {
  m <- reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~ sunday + saturday +", rhs, f)), d)
  list(sun = coef_of(m, "sunday"), sat = coef_of(m, "saturday"), n = if (is.null(m)) NA else nobs(m))
}
ivm <- function(y, d, inst = "sunday", exo = "saturday", rhs = cfor(d), f = fes(d), endo = "employment") {
  reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~", exo, "+", rhs, f, "|", endo, "~", inst)), d)
}
shr <- function(m, endo = "employment") {
  k <- coef_of(m, paste0("fit_", endo)); list(est = -k$est, se = k$se, p = k$p)
}
fsF <- function(m) tryCatch(unname(fitstat(m, "ivwald1")[[1]]$stat), error = function(e) NA_real_)

# ---- Groups (all derived columns are created on A before subsetting) ----
MR <- A[mgrp == "Regular salaried"]
MEN <- A[female == 0 & !is.na(mgrp)]
cM <- cfor(MR); FEr <- fes(MR)

# ---- Assignment of the diary day ----
day_share <- function(d) {
  s <- d[, .(w = sum(weight)), by = dow_f][, .(dow_f, sh = w / sum(w))]
  setNames(s$sh, as.character(s$dow_f))[names(CODE$day_of_week)]
}
days_all <- day_share(A); days_mr <- day_share(MR)
hh_same_day <- pd[, uniqueN(dow), by = hh_id][, mean(V1 == 1)]
fsu_vary <- A[, uniqueN(dow), by = fsu][, mean(V1 > 1)]

bal_lab <- c(age = "Age", female = "Female", married = "Currently married", never_married = "Never married",
             graduate = "Graduate or above", low_edu = "Not literate or below primary",
             urban = "Urban (sector)", hh_size = "Household size (all ages)", hh_n_under6 = "Members under 6",
             hh_n_6_14 = "Members aged 6--14", hh_n_60plus = "Members aged 60+",
             head_grad = "Head is a graduate", hh_max_grad = "Any member 15+ a graduate",
             hh_any_regular = "Any member regular salaried", hh_n_employed = "Members employed (usual status)",
             employed = "Employed (usual status)", regular = "Regular salaried (usual status)")
bal_lab <- bal_lab[vapply(names(bal_lab), function(v) has(A, v), logical(1))]
# Balance tests compare diaries within district x sub-round cells when both exist.
FEb <- if (has_dsr) fe(A, "dist_sr") else fes(A)
bal_fe_txt <- iff(has_dsr, "district-by-sub-round", fe_txt)
bal_one <- function(v, d) {
  m  <- reg(as.formula(paste(v, "~ sunday + saturday", FEb)), d)
  md <- reg(as.formula(paste(v, "~ i(dow)", FEb)), d)
  pj <- tryCatch(wald(md, keep = "^dow::", print = FALSE)$p, error = function(e) NA_real_)
  data.table(var = v, sun = coef_of(m, "sunday")$est, sun_se = coef_of(m, "sunday")$se,
             sun_p = coef_of(m, "sunday")$p, sat = coef_of(m, "saturday")$est,
             sat_se = coef_of(m, "saturday")$se, sat_p = coef_of(m, "saturday")$p, p_dow = pj)
}
bal <- rbindlist(lapply(names(bal_lab), bal_one, d = A))
joint_test <- function(d, vars, dep) {
  vars <- vars[vapply(vars, function(v) uniqueN(na.omit(d[[v]])) > 1, logical(1))]
  m <- reg(as.formula(paste(dep, "~", paste(vars, collapse = " + "), FEb)), d)
  w <- tryCatch(wald(m, keep = paste0("^(", paste(vars, collapse = "|"), ")$"), print = FALSE),
                error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(w)) list(stat = NA, p = NA) else list(stat = w$stat, p = w$p)
}
jt_sun_all <- joint_test(A, names(bal_lab), "sunday")
jt_sat_all <- joint_test(A, names(bal_lab), "saturday")
jt_sun_mr  <- joint_test(MR, setdiff(names(bal_lab), c("female", "employed", "regular", "hh_any_regular")), "sunday")
bal_ok <- isTRUE(jt_sun_all$p > 0.05) && isTRUE(jt_sun_mr$p > 0.05)
n_bal_sig <- sum(bal$sun_p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
k_proxy_sun <- if (has(MR, "proxy_report")) rf("proxy_report", MR, rhs = "1")$sun else list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA)
k_proxy_sat <- if (has(MR, "proxy_report")) rf("proxy_report", MR, rhs = "1")$sat else list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA)
# Type of day: is a Sunday diary more often an "other" (non-routine) day?
has_td <- has(MR, "type_day")
k_other_sun <- if (has_td) rf("other_day", MR, rhs = "1")$sun else list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA)
other_wk_mr <- if (has_td) wmean(MR[sunday == 0 & saturday == 0]$other_day, MR[sunday == 0 & saturday == 0]$weight) else NA
other_sun_mr <- if (has_td) wmean(MR[sunday == 1]$other_day, MR[sunday == 1]$weight) else NA
# Diaries by weekday (unweighted counts)
n_by_day <- A[, .N, by = dow_f][match(names(CODE$day_of_week), as.character(dow_f))]$N
n_by_day_all <- pd[, .N, by = dow_f][match(names(CODE$day_of_week), as.character(dow_f))]$N

# ---- Descriptives ----
dmean <- function(d, y, cond) wmean(d[cond][[y]], d[cond]$weight)

# ---- Paid work by diary day (figure) ----
byday <- rbindlist(lapply(c("Regular salaried", "Casual labour", "Self-employed"), function(g) {
  d <- A[mgrp == g]
  a <- as.data.table(est_mean(d, "employment", by = "dow_f"))[, panel := "Paid work (minutes)"]
  b <- as.data.table(est_mean(d, "no_work", by = "dow_f"))[, panel := "Share with no paid work"]
  x <- rbind(a, b); setnames(x, "group", "day"); x[, grp := g]; x
}))
zero_sun_mr <- dmean(MR, "no_work", MR$sunday == 1)
zero_wk_mr  <- dmean(MR, "no_work", MR$sunday == 0 & MR$saturday == 0)

# ---- First stage, reduced forms and IV for regular salaried men ----
k_fs <- rf("employment", MR)$sun; k_fs_sat <- rf("employment", MR)$sat
alloc_y <- c(ownuse_goods = "Own-use production of goods", unpaid_domestic = "Unpaid domestic services",
             unpaid_care = "Unpaid care for household members", volunteer = "Volunteer and other unpaid work",
             learning = "Learning", social_all = "Socialising, community, religion",
             leisure_all = "Culture, leisure, mass media, sport", selfcare_all = "Self-care and maintenance",
             sleep = "of which: sleep", unpaid = "Memo: all unpaid domestic and care",
             free_time = "Memo: free time (socialising + leisure)")
IV <- lapply(names(alloc_y), function(y) ivm(y, MR)); names(IV) <- names(alloc_y)
RFm <- lapply(names(alloc_y), function(y) rf(y, MR)$sun); names(RFm) <- names(alloc_y)
SH <- lapply(IV, shr)
fstat <- fsF(IV$unpaid)
share_sum <- sum(vapply(SH[setdiff(names(alloc_y), c("sleep", "unpaid", "free_time"))],
                        function(s) s$est, numeric(1)))
k_iv_unp <- SH$unpaid; k_iv_ft <- SH$free_time; k_iv_sl <- SH$sleep
k_rf_unp <- RFm$unpaid; k_rf_ft <- RFm$free_time; k_rf_sl <- RFm$sleep
unp_share <- k_iv_unp$est
sig_unp <- is_pos(k_iv_unp)
pass <- isTRUE(unp_share > 0.25)
strong_fs <- isTRUE(fstat > 10); very_strong_fs <- isTRUE(fstat > 104.7)
fs_neg <- is_neg(k_fs)
rest_share <- k_iv_ft$est + k_iv_sl$est
unp_below_rest <- isTRUE(unp_share < rest_share)

# ---- Tasks ----
task_y <- c(dom_food = "Food and meals", dom_cleaning = "Cleaning and upkeep",
            dom_textiles = "Care of textiles", dom_shopping = "Shopping",
            dom_repair = "Repair and maintenance", dom_management = "Household management",
            dom_misc = "Pets, domestic travel, other", care_child = "Childcare",
            care_adult = "Care of adults and other care")
TK <- rbindlist(lapply(names(task_y), function(y) {
  r <- rf(y, MR)$sun; s <- shr(ivm(y, MR))
  data.table(y = y, wk = dmean(MR, y, MR$sunday == 0 & MR$saturday == 0),
             rf = r$est, rf_se = r$se, rf_p = r$p, sh = s$est, sh_se = s$se)
}))
k_part <- rf("any_unpaid", MR)$sun
part_wk <- dmean(MR, "any_unpaid", MR$sunday == 0 & MR$saturday == 0)
top_task <- TK[which.max(sh)]$y
core_share <- sum(TK[y %in% c("dom_food", "dom_cleaning", "dom_textiles")]$sh, na.rm = TRUE)  # tasks nobody does contribute 0
male_share <- sum(TK[y %in% c("dom_shopping", "dom_repair", "dom_management")]$sh, na.rm = TRUE)

# ---- Saturday ----
iv_sat_unp <- ivm("unpaid", MR, inst = "saturday", exo = "sunday")
iv_sat_ft  <- ivm("free_time", MR, inst = "saturday", exo = "sunday")
iv_both    <- ivm("unpaid", MR, inst = "sunday + saturday", exo = "1")
k_sat_unp <- shr(iv_sat_unp); k_sat_ft <- shr(iv_sat_ft); k_both_unp <- shr(iv_both)
fstat_sat <- fsF(iv_sat_unp)
sargan_p <- tryCatch(unname(fitstat(iv_both, "sargan")[[1]]$p), error = function(e) NA_real_)
sat_fs_sig <- is_neg(k_fs_sat)
sat_smaller <- isTRUE(abs(k_fs_sat$est) < abs(k_fs$est))

# ---- Placebo groups ----
pl_groups <- c("Regular salaried", "Casual labour", "Self-employed", "Students", "Not in paid work")
pl_y <- c(employment = "Paid work", unpaid = "Unpaid domestic and care",
          free_time = "Free time", learning = "Learning")
PL <- rbindlist(lapply(pl_groups, function(g) {
  d <- A[mgrp == g]
  rbindlist(lapply(names(pl_y), function(y) {
    r <- rf(y, d)$sun
    data.table(group = g, y = y, est = r$est, se = r$se, p = r$p, n = nrow(d))
  }))
}))
plk <- function(g_, y_) { r <- PL[group == g_ & y == y_]; list(est = r$est, se = r$se, p = r$p) }
k_nw_unp <- plk("Not in paid work", "unpaid"); k_nw_emp <- plk("Not in paid work", "employment")
k_nw_ft  <- plk("Not in paid work", "free_time")
k_st_learn <- plk("Students", "learning")
k_cas_emp <- plk("Casual labour", "employment"); k_se_emp <- plk("Self-employed", "employment")
placebo_clean <- !is_sig(k_nw_unp)

# ---- Difference-in-reduced-forms IV (regular vs not-in-paid-work men) ----
PN <- A[mgrp %in% c("Regular salaried", "Not in paid work")]
cP <- cfor(PN); FEp <- fes(PN)
did_iv <- function(y) reg(as.formula(paste(y, "~ sunday + saturday + sat_reg + regular +", cP, FEp,
                                           "| employment ~ sun_reg")), PN)
k_did_unp <- shr(did_iv("unpaid")); k_did_ft <- shr(did_iv("free_time")); k_did_sl <- shr(did_iv("sleep"))
fstat_did <- fsF(did_iv("unpaid"))
did_close <- isTRUE(abs(k_did_unp$est - unp_share) < 1.96 * k_iv_unp$se)

# Sensitivity to a direct Sunday effect (Conley et al.): y - gamma * sunday
gam_grid <- seq(0, max(30, 5 * ceiling(2 * max(abs(c(k_rf_unp$est, k_nw_unp$est)), na.rm = TRUE) / 5)), length.out = 13)
Dg <- copy(MR)
SENS <- rbindlist(lapply(gam_grid, function(g) {
  Dg[, y_adj := unpaid - g * sunday]
  s <- shr(ivm("y_adj", Dg)); data.table(gamma = g, est = s$est, se = s$se)
}))
gamma_zero <- if (isTRUE(k_fs$est < 0)) k_rf_unp$est else NA  # direct effect at which share = 0

# ---- Heterogeneity among regular salaried men ----
het_def <- list(has_under6 = "Child under 6 in household", school_kid = "Child aged 6--14 in household",
                urban = "Urban", head_grad = "Household head a graduate",
                wife_emp = "Wife employed (usual status)")
het_def <- het_def[vapply(names(het_def), function(v) has(MR, v), logical(1))]
HET <- rbindlist(lapply(names(het_def), function(v) {
  d <- MR[!is.na(get(v))]
  d[, gg := as.integer(get(v) == 1)]
  d[, `:=`(emp_g = employment * gg, sun_g = sunday * gg, sat_g = saturday * gg)]
  mi <- reg(as.formula(paste("unpaid ~ saturday + sat_g + gg +", cfor(d), fes(d),
                             "| employment + emp_g ~ sunday + sun_g")), d)
  pdiff <- coef_of(mi, "fit_emp_g")$p
  rbindlist(lapply(c(1, 0), function(val) {
    s <- d[gg == val]
    fsk <- rf("employment", s)$sun
    iu <- shr(ivm("unpaid", s)); ifr <- shr(ivm("free_time", s))
    data.table(dim = het_def[[v]], level = ifelse(val == 1, "Yes", "No"), fs = fsk$est, fs_se = fsk$se,
               unp = iu$est, unp_se = iu$se, ft = ifr$est, ft_se = ifr$se,
               pdiff = if (val == 1) pdiff else NA_real_, n = nrow(s))
  }))
}))
het_sig <- HET[!is.na(pdiff) & pdiff < 0.05]$dim
hk <- function(dim_, lev) { r <- HET[dim == dim_ & level == lev]; list(est = r$unp, se = r$unp_se) }

# ---- Couples: wives of regular salaried men ----
H <- pd[, .(spouse_pid = pid, h_dow = dow, h_unpaid = unpaid_total, h_emp = employment,
            h_free = free_time, h_sleep = sleep, h_pas = pas_group)]
W0 <- pd[female == 1 & married == 1 & age >= 20 & age <= 59 & !is.na(spouse_pid)]
W0 <- merge(W0, H, by = "spouse_pid")
share_same_day <- W0[, mean(dow == h_dow)]
W0 <- W0[dow == h_dow]
W0[, `:=`(unpaid = unpaid_domestic + unpaid_care,
          c_unpaid = unpaid_domestic + unpaid_care + h_unpaid,
          gap = unpaid_domestic + unpaid_care - h_unpaid,
          h_share = fifelse(unpaid_domestic + unpaid_care + h_unpaid > 0,
                            h_unpaid / (unpaid_domestic + unpaid_care + h_unpaid), NA_real_),
          joint_free_ub = pmin(free_time, h_free),
          c_paid = employment + h_emp,
          h_reg = as.integer(h_pas == "Regular wage/salaried"),
          h_nw = as.integer(h_pas %in% c("Unemployed", "Domestic duties", "Other not working")))]
W0[, `:=`(sun_h = sunday * h_reg, sat_h = saturday * h_reg)]
CW <- c("i(age_band)", "i(edu_tier)", "urban", "hh_size",
        "hh_n_under6", "hh_n_6_14", "hh_n_60plus", "employed", SES_V)
Wv <- W0[h_reg == 1]
cW <- ctrl(Wv, CW); FEw <- fes(Wv)
rfw <- function(y, d = Wv) rf(y, d, rhs = ctrl(d, CW), f = fes(d))$sun
wy <- c(employment = "Wife: paid work", unpaid = "Wife: unpaid domestic and care",
        care_child = "Wife: childcare", free_time = "Wife: free time", sleep = "Wife: sleep",
        h_unpaid = "Husband: unpaid domestic and care", c_unpaid = "Couple: total unpaid work",
        gap = "Couple: wife minus husband unpaid work", h_share = "Couple: husband's share of unpaid work",
        joint_free_ub = "Couple: upper bound on joint free time", c_paid = "Couple: total paid work")
WT <- rbindlist(lapply(names(wy), function(y) {
  r <- rfw(y)
  data.table(y = y, wk = dmean(Wv, y, Wv$sunday == 0 & Wv$saturday == 0 & !is.na(Wv[[y]])),
             est = r$est, se = r$se, p = r$p)
}))
wk <- function(y_) { r <- WT[y == y_]; list(est = r$est, se = r$se, p = r$p) }
k_w_unp <- wk("unpaid"); k_w_ft <- wk("free_time"); k_w_emp <- wk("employment")
k_gap <- wk("gap"); k_hsh <- wk("h_share"); k_jf <- wk("joint_free_ub"); k_cu <- wk("c_unpaid")
gap_wk <- WT[y == "gap"]$wk; hsh_wk <- WT[y == "h_share"]$wk; jf_wk <- WT[y == "joint_free_ub"]$wk
k_h_fs <- rfw("h_emp")
k_w_iv <- shr(ivm("unpaid", Wv, rhs = cW, f = FEw, endo = "h_emp"), endo = "h_emp")
k_c_iv <- shr(ivm("c_unpaid", Wv, rhs = cW, f = FEw, endo = "h_emp"), endo = "h_emp")
# Wives of men not in paid work: the household's Sunday without the husband's day off
Wn <- W0[h_nw == 1]
k_wn_unp <- if (nrow(Wn) > 50) rfw("unpaid", Wn) else list(est = NA, se = NA, p = NA)
WD <- W0[h_reg == 1 | h_nw == 1]
k_wdid_unp <- coef_of(reg(as.formula(paste("unpaid ~ sunday + saturday + sun_h + sat_h + h_reg +",
                                           ctrl(WD, CW), fes(WD))), WD), "sun_h")
k_wdid_ft <- coef_of(reg(as.formula(paste("free_time ~ sunday + saturday + sun_h + sat_h + h_reg +",
                                          ctrl(WD, CW), fes(WD))), WD), "sun_h")
wives_down <- is_neg(k_w_unp); wives_up <- is_pos(k_w_unp)
gap_down <- is_neg(k_gap); gap_up <- is_pos(k_gap)

# ---- Robustness of the main IV ----
iv_unw <- function(y, d, rhs, f) tryCatch(feols(as.formula(paste(y, "~ saturday +", rhs, f, "| employment ~ sunday")),
                                               d, cluster = ~fsu), error = function(e) NULL)
rob_specs <- list(
  "Baseline" = list(d = MR, rhs = cM, f = FEr),
  "No controls (fixed effects only)" = list(d = MR, rhs = "1", f = FEr),
  "Adds proxy-report indicator" = if (has(MR, "proxy_report")) list(d = MR, rhs = paste(cM, "+ proxy_report"), f = FEr),
  "Self-reported diaries only" = if (has(MR, "proxy_report")) list(d = MR[proxy_report == 0], rhs = cfor(MR[proxy_report == 0]), f = FEr),
  "State instead of district fixed effects" = list(d = MR, rhs = cM, f = fe(MR, c("state", "sub_round"))),
  "District-by-sub-round fixed effects" = if (has_dsr) list(d = MR, rhs = cM, f = fe(MR, "dist_sr")),
  "FSU fixed effects" = list(d = MR, rhs = cM, f = fe(MR, c("fsu", "sub_round"))),
  "Normal days only (type of day)" = if (has_td) list(d = MR[type_day == CODE$type_of_day["normal"]],
                                                     rhs = cfor(MR[type_day == CODE$type_of_day["normal"]]), f = FEr),
  "Sunday against Monday--Friday only" = list(d = MR[saturday == 0], rhs = cM, f = FEr),
  "Married men only" = list(d = MR[married == 1], rhs = cfor(MR[married == 1]), f = FEr),
  "Unweighted" = list(d = MR, rhs = cM, f = FEr, unw = TRUE))
rob_specs <- rob_specs[!vapply(rob_specs, is.null, logical(1))]
ROB <- rbindlist(lapply(names(rob_specs), function(nm) {
  s <- rob_specs[[nm]]
  fit <- function(y) if (isTRUE(s$unw)) iv_unw(y, s$d, s$rhs, s$f) else ivm(y, s$d, rhs = s$rhs, f = s$f)
  mu <- fit("unpaid"); mf <- fit("free_time")
  fsk <- if (isTRUE(s$unw)) coef_of(tryCatch(feols(as.formula(paste("employment ~ sunday + saturday +", s$rhs, s$f)),
                                                 s$d, cluster = ~fsu), error = function(e) NULL), "sunday")
         else rf("employment", s$d, rhs = s$rhs, f = s$f)$sun
  data.table(spec = nm, fs = fsk$est, fs_se = fsk$se, F = fsF(mu),
             unp = shr(mu)$est, unp_se = shr(mu)$se, ft = shr(mf)$est, ft_se = shr(mf)$se,
             n = if (is.null(mu)) NA else nobs(mu))
}))
rob_range <- range(ROB$unp, na.rm = TRUE)
rob_stable <- isTRUE(all(abs(ROB$unp - unp_share) < 1.96 * k_iv_unp$se, na.rm = TRUE))

# ---- Additional quantities used in the text ----
share_reg <- A[female == 0 & employed == 1, wmean(regular, weight)]
n_mr <- nrow(MR); n_wv <- nrow(Wv); n_men <- nrow(MEN)
KD <- pd[age >= 6 & age <= 14 & pas_group == "Student"]
k_kid_learn <- rf("learning", KD, rhs = ctrl(KD, c("female", "urban", "hh_size", "i(head_edu_tier)", "i(hh_max_edu_tier)")))$sun
kid_learn_wk <- dmean(KD, "learning", KD$sunday == 0 & KD$saturday == 0)
iv_both_ft <- ivm("free_time", MR, inst = "sunday + saturday", exo = "1")
k_both_ft <- shr(iv_both_ft); fstat_both <- fsF(iv_both)
s100 <- function(k) f1(100 * k$est)
s100se <- function(k) f1(100 * k$se)
s100x <- function(k) paste0(s100(k), " (SE ", s100se(k), ")")
fs_wk_mr <- dmean(MR, "employment", MR$sunday == 0 & MR$saturday == 0)
unp_wk_mr <- dmean(MR, "unpaid", MR$sunday == 0 & MR$saturday == 0)
unp_wk_w <- dmean(Wv, "unpaid", Wv$sunday == 0 & Wv$saturday == 0)
```

\begin{abstract}
When men work fewer paid hours, do they take on unpaid work, or do they rest? Comparisons across men confound working time with selection into jobs and households. I use variation in men's paid work from the day of the week of the diary. India's Time Use Survey 2024 records each household member's diary for the day before the interview, and interviews are spread across the week, so the diary day varies across households within the same district and quarter. `r iff(bal_ok, "The pre-determined characteristics recorded in the file are balanced across diary days within district and quarter, consistent with, though not proof of, as-good-as-random assignment.", "Some pre-determined characteristics recorded in the file are not balanced across diary days, so the design relies on conditioning on them and on district and quarter fixed effects.")` `r iff(fs_neg, paste0("For regular salaried men, a Sunday diary reduces paid work by ", f0(abs(k_fs$est)), " minutes (SE ", f1(k_fs$se), ")."), paste0("For regular salaried men, a Sunday diary changes paid work by ", f0(k_fs$est), " minutes (SE ", f1(k_fs$se), "), so the design lacks a reliable first stage."))` Using the Sunday diary as an instrument for paid work, of every 100 minutes of paid work forgone, `r s100x(k_iv_unp)` go to unpaid domestic and care work, `r s100x(k_iv_ft)` to free time and `r s100x(k_iv_sl)` to sleep. `r iff(placebo_clean, "Among men without paid work, whose working day Sunday leaves unchanged, unpaid work does not change detectably on Sundays, which supports the exclusion restriction.", paste0("Among men without paid work, unpaid work also changes on Sundays; netting this direct Sunday effect out leaves ", s100x(k_did_unp), " minutes of unpaid work per 100 forgone."))` Wives of regular salaried men do `r diff_txt(k_w_unp)` unpaid work on the household's Sunday, and the wife-minus-husband gap in unpaid work, `r f0(gap_wk)` minutes on weekdays, is `r diff_txt(k_gap, "larger", "smaller")` on Sundays. `r iff(pass, "A substantial part of the time men are released from paid work flows into unpaid work, so shorter working hours could shift some unpaid work towards men.", "Men's time released from paid work flows mostly into leisure and rest, which bounds what shorter working hours alone can do for the gender division of unpaid work.")`
\keywords{weekend, working time, unpaid work, gender, time use, instrumental variables, India}
\jel{J22, J16, D13}
\end{abstract}

\newpage

# Introduction

Women in India do far more unpaid domestic and care work than men, and men do far more paid work [@hirway2011understanding; @nso2020tus; @nso2025tus]. One explanation for the gap is time availability: men do little at home because they are at work. The explanation has a long history in the sociology of housework [@coverman1985explaining; @shelton1996division; @coltrane2000research], and it is implicit in policies that try to change the division of unpaid work by changing men's working time, such as shorter standard weeks, flexible schedules and paternity leave. If time availability is the binding constraint, then releasing men from paid work should raise their unpaid work. If it is not, the released time should go mostly to leisure and rest, and the division of unpaid work should change little.

The question is hard to answer with a cross-section. Men who work fewer hours differ from men who work more in their jobs, health, wealth, family structure and attitudes, and each of these also predicts how much unpaid work they do. Evidence from economic shocks that cut men's working time, such as recessions, job loss and the COVID-19 lockdowns, shows that some of the released time goes to home production [@aguiar2013recession; @gough2011unemployment; @sevilla2020baby; @farre2022gender]. But these shocks also cut income, raise uncertainty and, in the case of lockdowns, close schools and keep every household member at home, so they do not isolate the effect of time itself.

This paper uses a cleaner and more ordinary source of variation: the day of the week. India's Time Use Survey (TUS) 2024 asks each household member aged six and over to report their activities for the 24 hours preceding the interview [@nso2025tus]. Interviews are spread over the week, so whether a household's diary falls on a Sunday, a Saturday or a weekday is set by when the investigator visits. For regular salaried men, most of whom have a fixed weekly day off, a Sunday diary removes most of a working day. If the visit schedule is unrelated to households' characteristics within a district and quarter, the diary day is a shock to these men's paid work that leaves their income, job and household unchanged. This is an assumption, which I test on the pre-determined characteristics the file records. Weekend comparisons have a long history in time-use research [@hamermesh2002timing; @jenkins2005nobody; @craig2014weekend]. What the TUS design adds is that the diary day is assigned by the survey calendar rather than chosen by the respondent, which makes it possible to use the weekend as an instrument.

I use the Sunday diary as an instrument for regular salaried men's paid work and estimate how a forgone minute of paid work is reallocated across every other activity. Because every diary sums to 1,440 minutes, the instrumental-variables (IV) coefficients for the non-work activities sum to one, and each is the share of a forgone paid-work minute that goes to that activity. The sample contains `r fn(n_mr)` diaries of regular salaried men aged 20 to 59. `r iff(fs_neg, paste0("A Sunday diary reduces their paid work by ", diff_txt(list(est = -abs(k_fs$est), se = k_fs$se), "", "", 0), "from a weekday mean of ", f0(fs_wk_mr), " minutes, and the share with no paid work at all is ", pct(zero_sun_mr), " on Sundays against ", pct(zero_wk_mr), " on weekdays."), paste0("A Sunday diary changes their paid work by ", est_se(k_fs), ", which is not a usable first stage."))` `r iff(very_strong_fs, paste0("The first-stage F statistic is ", f0(fstat), ", far above the threshold at which conventional IV inference is reliable [@lee2022valid]."), iff(strong_fs, paste0("The first-stage F statistic is ", f0(fstat), ", above conventional thresholds but below the level at which conventional t-tests need no adjustment [@lee2022valid]."), paste0("The first-stage F statistic is ", f1(fstat), ", so the IV estimates should be read with caution [@andrews2019weak].")))`

Four findings stand out. First, of every 100 minutes of paid work forgone on Sunday, `r s100x(k_iv_unp)` go to unpaid domestic and care work, `r s100x(k_iv_ft)` to free time (socialising, leisure, media and sport) and `r s100x(k_iv_sl)` to sleep. The unpaid-work share is `r iff(sig_unp, "positive and statistically significant", "not statistically distinguishable from zero at the 5% level")`, and it is `r iff(unp_below_rest, "smaller", "larger")` than the combined share that goes to free time and sleep. Second, the unpaid work that men do take on is concentrated in particular tasks: the largest share goes to `r tolower(task_y[top_task])`. Third, several tests support the exclusion restriction that Sunday affects men's unpaid work only through their paid work. `r iff(bal_ok, paste0("Pre-determined characteristics are balanced across diary days within district and quarter (joint p = ", f2(jt_sun_all$p), ")."), paste0("Pre-determined characteristics are only partly balanced across diary days (joint p = ", f2(jt_sun_all$p), " for all persons and ", f2(jt_sun_mr$p), " for regular salaried men), so conditioning on them matters."))` `r iff(placebo_clean, "Among men without paid work, for whom Sunday changes nothing at work, unpaid work does not change detectably on Sundays.", "Among men without paid work, unpaid work does change on Sundays, which points to a direct effect of the day; I net it out with a difference-in-reduced-forms IV.")` The net estimate is `r s100x(k_did_unp)` minutes per 100. Fourth, wives of regular salaried men do `r diff_txt(k_w_unp)` unpaid work on the household's Sunday, and the wife-minus-husband gap in unpaid work is `r diff_txt(k_gap, "larger", "smaller")` on Sundays than its weekday level of `r f0(gap_wk)` minutes.

The paper makes three contributions. It provides a quasi-experimental estimate of the marginal allocation of men's paid-work time in a low-income, high-gap setting, whereas the causal studies of working time and housework reviewed below are from high-income countries [@goux2014worktime; @kawaguchi2013gift; @patnaik2019reserving]. It shows how a common feature of time-use survey design, the "yesterday" diary combined with interviews spread over the week, can be used for identification, with a set of falsification tests that other surveys with the same design can reproduce. And it links the husband's response to the wife's response within the same couple on the same day, which speaks directly to whether shorter working time redistributes unpaid work or only adds leisure.

The rest of the paper proceeds as follows. Section \ref{sec:lit} reviews the literature. Section \ref{sec:framework} sets out a simple framework. Section \ref{sec:data} describes the data and Section \ref{sec:strategy} the design. Section \ref{sec:results} presents the results, Section \ref{sec:discussion} discusses interpretation and policy, and Section \ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

# Related literature {#sec:lit}

## Total work, time availability and the division of unpaid work

The economic analysis of time use begins with the household as a producer that combines market goods and members' time [@becker1965theory], with specialisation by comparative advantage [@becker1991treatise] and, in later models, with bargaining between spouses whose outside options shape the allocation [@lundberg1993separate]. In these models a fall in one spouse's market hours, holding wages fixed, should raise that spouse's home production, by an amount that depends on how substitutable spouses' home time is and on how much the released time is valued as leisure.

Descriptive work on total work, the sum of paid and unpaid work, finds that men and women in rich countries do similar amounts of total work, while in poorer countries women's total work tends to exceed men's [@burda2013total]. Over the long run, women's paid work has risen and their unpaid work has fallen, while men's unpaid work has risen slowly [@gershuny2000changing; @bianchi2000anyone; @sayer2005gender; @gimenez2012trends; @aguiar2007measuring]. Convergence has been uneven across countries and tasks. Men's participation has risen more in some institutional settings than in others [@gershuny2003time; @hook2006care; @kan2011gender], and the segregation of housework into "male" and "female" tasks has persisted [@hook2010gender].

Sociologists distinguish three explanations for the division of housework: time availability, relative resources and gender ideology [@coverman1985explaining; @shelton1996division; @coltrane2000research]. Time availability predicts that each spouse's housework falls with their own paid hours. Relative resources predicts that the spouse with more earnings or bargaining power does less. Gender ideology and identity predict that norms about what men and women should do constrain the division regardless of time or money. The evidence that husbands who are economically dependent on their wives do less, not more, housework [@brines1994economic], that women's housework declines with their relative earnings only up to a point [@bittman2003gender], and that couples in which the wife out-earns the husband show patterns consistent with gender identity [@akerlof2000identity; @bertrand2015identity] all suggest that time availability is not the whole story. These studies, however, rely on cross-sectional or panel variation in hours and earnings that is itself chosen. The design here holds income, job and household fixed and moves only time.

## What people do with released time

A body of work estimates how time released from paid work is reallocated. @aguiar2013recession use the American Time Use Survey over the Great Recession and find that roughly 30 percent of forgone market work hours were reallocated to home production and about half to leisure, much of it sleep and television. @burda2010unemployment compare the time use of the unemployed and the employed across countries, and @gough2011unemployment study how men's and women's housework changes with unemployment within couples. Retirement offers a further, predictable reduction in working time, and @stancanelli2012retirement use a regression discontinuity at retirement age to estimate its effect on home production. Each of these shocks changes more than time: unemployment and recessions cut income and raise uncertainty, and retirement is permanent and anticipated.

Working-time regulation is closer to the experiment of interest. @goux2014worktime study the French reduction of the standard work week to 35 hours and find that the reduction in husbands' hours also reduced their wives' hours, consistent with complementarity in spouses' leisure. @kawaguchi2013gift study how Japanese and Korean workers reallocated time when statutory standard hours were cut, and @hamermesh2017labor examine workers' well-being after the Korean reduction. In a closely related use of day-to-day variation, @connolly2008rain shows that men in the United States substitute between work and leisure across rainy and dry days. The present paper uses a different, recurring and plausibly exogenous source of variation, the weekly day off, in a country where men's baseline unpaid work is very low.

## Paternity leave and men's care

Paternity leave is the policy most directly aimed at men's unpaid work. Reserved "father quotas" raise fathers' leave-taking substantially. Their longer-run effects on the division of unpaid work are mixed. Exposure to the Norwegian quota is associated with a more equal division of some housework tasks and less conflict over housework [@kotsadam2011state]. The Quebec quota raised fathers' later time in household production [@patnaik2019reserving]. German fathers who take leave are more involved in childcare afterwards [@tamm2019fathers]. The Swedish "daddy month", by contrast, raised fathers' leave-taking but did not detectably change how parents later shared leave to care for sick children [@ekberg2013parental]. Paternity leave combines released time with an explicit expectation of care, and often a period alone in charge of an infant. A day off has only the first element. Comparing the two is informative about whether time or expectation is the binding constraint.

## The COVID-19 lockdowns

The lockdowns of 2020 were a large and sudden reduction in many men's paid work. In the United Kingdom, fathers' childcare rose, especially where the father stopped working, and the gender gap in childcare narrowed modestly [@sevilla2020baby; @hupkau2020work]. In Spain, men's participation in housework and childcare rose somewhat, but women continued to do most of it [@farre2022gender]. @alon2020impact argued that the lockdowns could shift norms because many fathers were in charge of childcare for the first time. In India, men's reported hours of domestic work rose during the 2020 lockdown, while women continued to do far more [@deshpande2020covid]. The lockdowns, however, also closed schools, removed paid domestic help and confined every household member to the home, so the increase in men's unpaid work mixes the effect of time with a large increase in the total amount of unpaid work to be done.

## Timing, synchronisation and the weekend

A separate literature studies when, rather than how much, people work. Spouses value time together and coordinate the timing of their work and leisure [@hamermesh2002timing; @hallberg2003synchronous]. The value of leisure depends on whether others are free at the same time [@jenkins2005nobody], and spouses' non-market time choices depend on each other's [@connelly2009spousal]. Non-standard schedules reduce the time couples and families spend together [@presser2003working; @lesnard2008off]. When dual-earner spouses work different shifts, husbands do more of the tasks traditionally done by women [@presser1994employment]. @craig2011nonstandard study how non-standard schedules relate to the division of childcare, and @craig2014weekend show that weekend work reduces leisure time with family and friends, with different costs for men and women. @bryan2017flexible examine whether flexible working helps couples coordinate their time, and @hamermesh2015long document that Americans work at nights and on weekends more often than Europeans.

The weekend therefore has two distinct roles. It releases time, and it synchronises: when the husband's day off coincides with children's school holiday and with other households' days off, the household is together, and the released time may be used jointly rather than in unpaid work. This makes the weekend an informative experiment for policy, because shorter working weeks would usually be implemented as longer weekends.

## Men's unpaid work in India

India's gender gap in unpaid work is large and persistent. It is documented in the 1998--99 pilot time-use survey [@hirway2011understanding], the TUS 2019 [@nso2020tus] and the TUS 2024 [@nso2025tus]. The gap coexists with low and stagnant female labour force participation [@klasen2015stagnation; @afridi2018married; @chatterjee2018indian; @fletcher2017women]. Social norms about women's work outside the home are a central explanation [@jayachandran2021social], and interventions that change women's control over earnings can shift both labour supply and norms [@field2021account]. Norms about men's unpaid work have received less attention. Experimental evidence from other settings shows that men can misperceive the norms held by their peers [@bursztyn2020misperceived], which suggests that men's unpaid work may respond to the visibility of other men's behaviour as well as to time. This paper asks the prior question: whether, when the constraint of paid work is lifted for a day, Indian men use the time for unpaid work at all.

# A simple framework {#sec:framework}

Let a man's day of $T = 1{,}440$ minutes be divided into paid work $h$ and $K$ other activities $a_1, \ldots, a_K$, so that $h + \sum_k a_k = T$. On a working day, $h$ is set largely by the employer. On a day off, $h$ falls by $\Delta h < 0$ for reasons unrelated to the man's preferences that day. The time constraint implies

$$ \sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{\Delta a_k}{-\Delta h} = 1. $$

Each term $s_k = \Delta a_k / (-\Delta h)$ is the share of a forgone paid-work minute allocated to activity $k$. Time availability predicts a large share for unpaid work $s_u$. A model in which men's unpaid work is fixed by norms or by the division of tasks within the household predicts $s_u \approx 0$, with the released time going to leisure and sleep.

The wife's response is informative about how spouses' time interacts. If spouses' unpaid work is substitutable, the wife's unpaid work falls when the husband's rises, and the within-couple gap narrows by more than the husband's increase. If spouses value joint leisure [@hamermesh2002timing; @goux2014worktime], the wife's free time rises on the husband's day off and her unpaid work may fall even when his does not rise. If the household's demand for unpaid work rises on Sundays, because children are at home or because weekly tasks are done on the day off, both spouses' unpaid work rises. The data distinguish these cases by the joint sign pattern of the wife's unpaid work, her free time and the husband's unpaid work.

Two features of a day off differ from a permanent reduction in working time. A day off is anticipated and recurs weekly, so tasks that can be postponed, such as shopping or repairs, may be moved to it from other days. This intertemporal reallocation would make the Sunday share of unpaid work larger than the share under a permanent reduction. A day off is also a common holiday for children and many other workers. This synchronisation would make leisure more valuable on Sundays than on a day off taken alone, and the Sunday share of leisure larger than under a staggered reduction. Section \ref{sec:discussion} returns to these points.

# Data {#sec:data}

## The Time Use Survey 2024

The TUS 2024 was conducted by the National Statistics Office from January to December 2024 [@nso2025tus]. It covers a nationally representative sample of households, and every member aged six and over reports their activities in 30-minute slots for the 24 hours from 4 a.m. on the day before the interview. Activities are coded to the International Classification of Activities for Time-Use Statistics 2016 [@un2016icatus]. The analysis uses every activity record (`r fn(V$n_rows)` records, `r fn(V$n_persons)` diaries in `r fn(V$n_households)` households), aggregated to one row per person-day. Minutes are computed from major activities, so every diary sums to 1,440 minutes (Appendix Table \ref{tab:validation}). All estimates use the survey weights and cluster standard errors on the first-stage unit (FSU), the primary sampling unit [@abadie2023cluster; @cameron2015practitioner; @solon2015weighting].

`r data_disclosure(V)` For this paper the missing household items matter mainly as controls and balance checks: the design does not need them, but I cannot test balance on consumption, caste or religion. Besides the roster, the file records for each diary its day of the week, the survey sub-round (quarter) in which the household was visited, the district, whether the respondent described the day as a "normal" or an "other" day, and the serial number of the household member who reported the diary, from which I identify proxy-reported diaries. Each member's own diary day is recorded, so spouses' diary days can be compared directly.

The outcome categories follow the ICATUS divisions: employment and related activities (paid work, including work-related travel and commuting); production of goods for own final use; unpaid domestic services; unpaid caregiving for household members; volunteer and other unpaid work; learning; socialising, community participation and religious practice; culture, leisure, mass media and sport; and self-care and maintenance, which includes sleep. "Unpaid work" is the sum of unpaid domestic services and unpaid care, the SDG 5.4.1 definition. "Free time" is the sum of socialising and leisure. Unpaid domestic work is split into its ICATUS sub-divisions to study which tasks men take on.

## Samples

The main sample is men aged 20 to 59 whose usual principal activity status is regular wage or salaried employment, who make up `r pct(share_reg)` of employed men in this age range. They are the group for whom the weekly day off is most clearly set by the employer. Indian labour law requires a weekly holiday for factory workers, by default on the first day of the week (Factories Act, 1948, Section 52). Figure \ref{fig:fig-byday} shows how paid work varies by diary day in the data. Placebo samples are men of the same age who are casual labourers, self-employed, students, or not in paid work (unemployed, attending to domestic duties, or otherwise out of the labour force). The couple sample links wives aged 20 to 59 to their husbands through the household roster (head and spouse, or married child and child's spouse). In `r pct(share_same_day)` of linked couples both spouses' diaries refer to the same day; I keep these couples, of whom `r fn(n_wv)` have a regular salaried husband, so that both spouses' outcomes refer to the same day.

```{r tab-desc}
dsc_y <- c(employment = "Paid work", unpaid_domestic = "Unpaid domestic services", unpaid_care = "Unpaid care",
           free_time = "Free time", sleep = "Sleep", any_unpaid = "Any unpaid work (share)")
cell <- function(d, y, cond) { x <- dmean(d, y, cond); if (y == "any_unpaid") f2(x) else f0(x) }
WvA <- copy(Wv); WvA[, any_unpaid := as.integer(unpaid > 0)]
dd <- data.frame(Outcome = c(dsc_y, "Diaries"),
  `Men Mon--Fri` = c(sapply(names(dsc_y), function(y) cell(MR, y, MR$sunday == 0 & MR$saturday == 0)), fn(sum(MR$sunday == 0 & MR$saturday == 0))),
  `Men Sat` = c(sapply(names(dsc_y), function(y) cell(MR, y, MR$saturday == 1)), fn(sum(MR$saturday == 1))),
  `Men Sun` = c(sapply(names(dsc_y), function(y) cell(MR, y, MR$sunday == 1)), fn(sum(MR$sunday == 1))),
  `Wives Mon--Fri` = c(sapply(names(dsc_y), function(y) cell(WvA, y, WvA$sunday == 0 & WvA$saturday == 0)), fn(sum(WvA$sunday == 0 & WvA$saturday == 0))),
  `Wives Sat` = c(sapply(names(dsc_y), function(y) cell(WvA, y, WvA$saturday == 1)), fn(sum(WvA$saturday == 1))),
  `Wives Sun` = c(sapply(names(dsc_y), function(y) cell(WvA, y, WvA$sunday == 1)), fn(sum(WvA$sunday == 1))),
  check.names = FALSE)
tab(dd, caption = paste0("Minutes per day by diary day: regular salaried men 20--59 and their wives", syn_note()),
    label = "desc", align = c("l", rep("r", 6)),
    notes = "Survey-weighted means. Wives are linked spouses of regular salaried men whose diaries refer to the same day as their husband's. Free time is socialising, community and religious activities plus culture, leisure, mass media and sport.")
```

Table \ref{tab:desc} shows the raw contrast. Regular salaried men work `r f0(fs_wk_mr)` paid minutes on an average weekday and do `r f0(unp_wk_mr)` minutes of unpaid work; their wives do `r f0(unp_wk_w)` minutes of unpaid work. The columns for Sunday show how both spouses' days change when the husband's working day is removed.

# Empirical strategy {#sec:strategy}

## Assignment of the diary day

The diary refers to the day before the interview, and the interview date is set by the investigator's schedule within the FSU. If that schedule is unrelated to households' characteristics, conditional on district and survey sub-round, the diary day is as good as randomly assigned. This cannot be verified directly, but two features of the data are consistent with it. Diary days are spread evenly over the week (Appendix Table \ref{tab:days}): each day of the week has between `r fn(min(n_by_day_all, na.rm = TRUE))` and `r fn(max(n_by_day_all, na.rm = TRUE))` diaries, and the weighted share of diaries of persons aged 20 to 59 on each day lies between `r pct(min(days_all, na.rm = TRUE))` and `r pct(max(days_all, na.rm = TRUE))`. The diary day also varies within FSUs: in `r pct(fsu_vary)` of FSUs, sampled households report on more than one day. Within households, `r pct(hh_same_day)` of households have all members' diaries on the same day, so the diary day is in practice a household-level assignment.

The main threat to assignment is that investigators might find some households at home only on particular days. Households in which the man works on weekdays might be interviewed disproportionately on Mondays (diary day Sunday) or on Sundays (diary day Saturday), for example. Table \ref{tab:balance} tests this by regressing pre-determined characteristics on Sunday and Saturday indicators with `r bal_fe_txt` fixed effects, so that diaries are compared only with others from the same district and quarter. It reports a joint test of all six day-of-week indicators for each characteristic, and a joint test of all characteristics in a regression of the Sunday indicator on them. The characteristics are those the person-level file records: age, sex, education, marital status, household size and composition (including children under six from the roster), sector, and the roster-based socioeconomic proxies (the head's education, the highest education in the household, whether any member is regular salaried and the number of employed members). Usual activity status refers to the past year and does not depend on the diary day.

## Instrumental variables

For regular salaried men I estimate

$$ y_i = \theta\, h_i + \beta\, Sat_i + X_i'\gamma + \mu_{s} + u_i, \qquad h_i = \pi\, Sun_i + \rho\, Sat_i + X_i'\delta + \mu_{s} + v_i, $$

where $h_i$ is minutes of paid work, $y_i$ is minutes in another activity, $Sun_i$ and $Sat_i$ indicate the diary day, $X_i$ contains age band, education, marital status, urban residence, household size, the numbers of household members under 6, aged 6 to 14 and aged 60 or over, and the socioeconomic proxies (head's education, highest education in the household, any regular salaried member, number of employed members), and $\mu_s$ are `r fe_txt` fixed effects. District fixed effects absorb local differences in income, caste composition, infrastructure and market days that the file does not measure; sub-round fixed effects absorb seasonality, including the agricultural calendar and the timing of festivals. Saturday enters as a control, so the instrument contrasts Sunday with Monday to Friday. The share of a forgone paid-work minute allocated to activity $y$ is $s_y = -\theta$. Because the outcomes partition the day, the estimated shares across the eight non-employment ICATUS divisions sum to exactly one (here, `r f2(share_sum)`).

Under monotonicity, the IV estimate is a local average effect for compliers [@imbens1994late; @angrist2009mostly]: regular salaried men who work on weekdays and not on Sundays. Men who work every day, and men who would not have worked that weekday anyway, do not contribute. This is the population of interest for a policy that shortens the standard working week of salaried employees.

I report the first-stage Wald F statistic computed with the clustered variance, which equals the effective F of @montiel2013robust with a single instrument. When it exceeds 104.7, the conventional 5% t-test has correct size without adjustment [@lee2022valid].

The outcomes contain many zeros, since many men do no unpaid work on a given day. I estimate linear models in minutes, which recover population means of time use without the distributional assumptions of censored models [@stewart2013tobit]. Single-day diaries measure time on a day, not a person's typical day [@frazis2012think]. Here this is the point: the estimand is the response of a day's time use to that day's paid work.

## The exclusion restriction

The exclusion restriction requires that Sunday affects a regular salaried man's unpaid work only through his paid work. Four channels could violate it. (i) Other household members are also at home on Sundays: children are out of school and wives who work are off. Their presence changes the amount of unpaid work to be done and who is available to do it. (ii) Markets and services operate differently on Sundays: some shops close and weekly markets meet on fixed days. (iii) Religious and social activities are concentrated on particular days. (iv) Reporting differs by day: a Sunday diary is reported on a Monday, when the man is more likely to be at work and to have his diary reported by another household member. These channels mostly operate through the household's day, not the man's job, so they should also be present for men whose paid work does not change on Sundays.

I test this in three ways. The falsification test estimates the Sunday effect on unpaid work among men aged 20 to 59 who are not in paid work. For them, Sunday changes nothing at work, so any Sunday effect on their unpaid work is a direct effect of the day. Students provide a second placebo group, and the Sunday effect on children's learning time measures how much the school calendar changes the household's day. Second, a difference-in-reduced-forms IV pools regular salaried men with men not in paid work and uses the interaction of Sunday and regular salaried status as the instrument, controlling for Sunday and Saturday main effects and for status. This removes any direct Sunday effect that is common to the two groups. Third, I report how the estimated unpaid-work share changes under an assumed direct Sunday effect of $\gamma$ minutes, by re-estimating the IV with $y_i - \gamma\, Sun_i$ as the outcome [@conley2012plausibly].

Casual labourers and the self-employed are not clean placebos: Sunday can reduce their paid work too, but less predictably. Their first stages show how specific the weekly day off is to salaried employment. The Saturday indicator serves as a second instrument. Many salaried men work a full or half day on Saturdays, so Saturday is a weaker but distinct shock, and the comparison of Saturday and Sunday IV estimates tests whether the allocation of released time depends on which day is released.

# Results {#sec:results}

## Balance

```{r tab-balance}
bt <- data.frame(Characteristic = bal_lab[bal$var],
                 Sunday = paste0(f2(bal$sun), stars(bal$sun_p)), `SE ` = f2(bal$sun_se),
                 Saturday = paste0(f2(bal$sat), stars(bal$sat_p)), SE = f2(bal$sat_se),
                 `p, all days` = f2(bal$p_dow), check.names = FALSE)
bt <- rbind(bt, data.frame(Characteristic = c("Joint test, all characteristics (p): all persons",
                                              "Joint test, all characteristics (p): regular salaried men"),
                           Sunday = c(f2(jt_sun_all$p), f2(jt_sun_mr$p)), `SE ` = "",
                           Saturday = c(f2(jt_sat_all$p), ""), SE = "", `p, all days` = "", check.names = FALSE))
tab(bt, caption = paste0("Balance of pre-determined characteristics by diary day", syn_note()), label = "balance",
    align = c("l", rep("r", 5)),
    notes = paste0("Persons 20--59 (", fn(nrow(A)), " diaries). Each row regresses the characteristic on Sunday and Saturday indicators (Monday to Friday omitted) with ", bal_fe_txt, " fixed effects. 'p, all days' is the p-value of a joint Wald test that all six day-of-week indicators are zero. The joint tests regress the Sunday (Saturday) indicator on all listed characteristics and test that their coefficients are jointly zero. FSU-clustered SEs. * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01."))
```

Table \ref{tab:balance} `r iff(bal_ok, "is consistent with as-good-as-random assignment of the diary day within district and quarter.", "supports as-good-as-random assignment only in part.")` Of `r length(bal_lab)` characteristics, `r n_bal_sig` `r iff(n_bal_sig == 1, "differs", "differ")` between Sunday and weekday diaries at the 5% level, against `r f1(0.05 * length(bal_lab))` expected by chance. The joint test that all characteristics are unrelated to a Sunday diary has p = `r f2(jt_sun_all$p)` for all persons and p = `r f2(jt_sun_mr$p)` among regular salaried men. `r iff(bal_ok, "Neither rejects, so the observed characteristics that predict unpaid work are not associated with the diary day. Balance on unobserved characteristics, including consumption, caste and religion, which the file does not record, cannot be tested.", "At least one rejects at the 5% level, so the controls and the robustness checks with FSU fixed effects carry more weight than they would under clean assignment.")` All estimates condition on these characteristics.

The design does predict one feature that is not pre-determined: who reports the diary. A Sunday diary is collected on a Monday, when salaried men are more likely to be at work. Among regular salaried men, a diary is `r diff_pp(k_proxy_sun, "more", "less")` likely to have been reported by another household member when it refers to a Sunday, and `r diff_pp(k_proxy_sat, "more", "less")` likely when it refers to a Saturday, which is collected on a Sunday. Proxy reporting is therefore an outcome of the design rather than a control. I exclude it from the main specification and show results with it as a control and for self-reported diaries only. `r iff(has_td, paste0("The type of day is not pre-determined either. Among regular salaried men, ", pct(other_wk_mr), " of weekday diaries and ", pct(other_sun_mr), " of Sunday diaries are described as an \"other\" rather than a normal day (Sunday difference ", diff_pp(k_other_sun), "). If weekly days off are classed as other days, restricting to normal days removes part of the variation the design uses; I therefore report it only as a robustness check."), "")`

```{r fig-byday, fig.cap = paste0("Paid work by diary day: men 20--59 by usual activity status", syn_note()), fig.height = 3.4}
byday[, `:=`(grp = factor(grp, levels = c("Regular salaried", "Casual labour", "Self-employed")),
             day = factor(day, levels = names(CODE$day_of_week)))]
ggplot(byday, aes(day, est, colour = grp, group = grp)) +

  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = est - 1.96 * se, ymax = est + 1.96 * se), size = 0.2) +
```
