Figure \ref{fig:fig-byday} plots mean paid work and the share of men with no paid work by diary day. `r iff(fs_neg, paste0("For regular salaried men, paid work is flat from Monday to Friday and falls sharply on Sunday; the share doing no paid work rises from ", pct(zero_wk_mr), " on weekdays to ", pct(zero_sun_mr), " on Sundays."), "For regular salaried men, paid work does not fall clearly on Sundays.")` Casual labourers' paid work changes by `r est_se(k_cas_emp)` on Sundays and self-employed men's by `r est_se(k_se_emp)`. `r iff(isTRUE(abs(k_cas_emp$est) < abs(k_fs$est) & abs(k_se_emp$est) < abs(k_fs$est)), "Both are smaller than the change for salaried men, consistent with the weekly day off being a feature of salaried employment.", "At least one is as large as the change for salaried men, so the Sunday day off is not specific to salaried employment in these data.")`

## How men reallocate released time

```{r tab-iv}
iv_tab <- data.frame(Activity = unname(alloc_y),
  `Weekday mean` = sapply(names(alloc_y), function(y) f0(dmean(MR, y, MR$sunday == 0 & MR$saturday == 0))),
  `Sunday effect (min)` = sapply(RFm, function(k) paste0(f1(k$est), stars(k$p))),
  `SE ` = sapply(RFm, function(k) f1(k$se)),
  `Share of forgone minute` = sapply(SH, function(k) paste0(formatC(k$est, format = "f", digits = 3), stars(k$p))),
  SE = sapply(SH, function(k) formatC(k$se, format = "f", digits = 3)), check.names = FALSE)
iv_tab <- rbind(data.frame(Activity = "Paid work (first stage)", `Weekday mean` = f0(fs_wk_mr),
                           `Sunday effect (min)` = paste0(f1(k_fs$est), stars(k_fs$p)), `SE ` = f1(k_fs$se),
                           `Share of forgone minute` = "", SE = "", check.names = FALSE), iv_tab)
tab(iv_tab, caption = paste0("Allocation of paid-work time forgone on Sunday: regular salaried men 20--59", syn_note()),
    label = "iv", align = c("l", rep("r", 5)),
    notes = paste0("N = ", fn(n_mr), ". 'Sunday effect' is the reduced-form coefficient on a Sunday diary (Saturday, controls and fixed effects included). 'Share of forgone minute' is minus the 2SLS coefficient on paid work, instrumented by the Sunday diary. The shares of the eight ICATUS divisions sum to ", f2(share_sum), ". First-stage F = ", f0(fstat), ". FSU-clustered SEs. * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01."))
```

Table \ref{tab:iv} reports the reduced form and the IV allocation. Of every 100 minutes of paid work forgone on Sunday, `r s100x(k_iv_unp)` go to unpaid domestic and care work, `r s100x(k_iv_ft)` to free time and `r s100x(k_iv_sl)` to sleep. The remainder goes to own-use production, volunteering, learning and self-care other than sleep. In minutes, a Sunday changes these men's unpaid work by `r est_se(k_rf_unp)`, their free time by `r est_se(k_rf_ft)` and their sleep by `r est_se(k_rf_sl)`. `r iff(sig_unp, paste0("The unpaid-work share is positive and statistically significant, and its 95% confidence interval, ", ci95(list(est = 100 * k_iv_unp$est, se = 100 * k_iv_unp$se)), " minutes per 100, excludes zero."), paste0("The unpaid-work share is not statistically distinguishable from zero; its 95% confidence interval is ", ci95(list(est = 100 * k_iv_unp$est, se = 100 * k_iv_unp$se)), " minutes per 100."))` `r iff(pass, "More than a quarter of the released time goes to unpaid work, a substantial response by the standard of the recession evidence for the United States [@aguiar2013recession].", "Less than a quarter of the released time goes to unpaid work, a smaller share than the roughly 30 percent of forgone market hours that went to home production in the United States during the Great Recession [@aguiar2013recession], although the two shocks differ in duration and in their effect on income.")`

The released time is `r iff(unp_below_rest, "used mainly", "not used mainly")` for rest and leisure: the combined share of free time and sleep is `r s100(list(est = rest_share))` minutes per 100, `r iff(unp_below_rest, "larger", "smaller")` than the unpaid-work share.

## Which unpaid tasks

```{r tab-tasks}
tt <- data.frame(Task = unname(task_y[TK$y]), `Weekday mean` = f1(TK$wk),
                 `Sunday effect (min)` = paste0(f1(TK$rf), stars(TK$rf_p)), SE = f1(TK$rf_se),
                 `Per 100 min forgone` = f1(100 * TK$sh), `SE ` = f1(100 * TK$sh_se), check.names = FALSE)
tab(tt, caption = paste0("Unpaid tasks taken on when paid work is released: regular salaried men 20--59", syn_note()),
    label = "tasks", align = c("l", rep("r", 5)),
    notes = "Reduced-form Sunday coefficients and 2SLS shares (minus the coefficient on paid work instrumented by Sunday, times 100) for ICATUS sub-divisions of unpaid domestic services and unpaid care. '--' marks tasks with no variation in the sample. Controls and fixed effects as in the baseline allocation table. FSU-clustered SEs. * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01.")
```

Table \ref{tab:tasks} splits unpaid work into tasks. The largest share of the released time that goes to unpaid work is spent on `r tolower(task_y[top_task])` (`r f1(100 * TK[y == top_task]$sh)` minutes per 100). Routine, traditionally female tasks (food preparation, cleaning and the care of textiles) together absorb `r f1(100 * core_share)` minutes per 100, against `r f1(100 * male_share)` for shopping, repairs and household management, tasks that are more often shared or done by men [@hook2010gender]. `r iff(isTRUE(male_share > core_share), "The response is thus concentrated in tasks that can be batched into a weekly day off and that do not displace the wife's daily routine.", "The response is thus not confined to the tasks men already do.")` The share of men doing any unpaid work, `r pct(part_wk)` on weekdays, is `r diff_pp(k_part)` on Sundays, so `r iff(is_sig(k_part), "part of the response is on the extensive margin", "the response is mostly on the intensive margin, among men who already do some unpaid work")`.

## Saturday as a separate shock

```{r tab-alt}
alt <- data.frame(Specification = c("Sunday instrument (baseline)", "Saturday instrument", "Sunday and Saturday instruments",
                                     "Difference-in-reduced-forms (regular vs. not in paid work)"),
                  `Unpaid work per 100 min` = c(s100(k_iv_unp), s100(k_sat_unp), s100(k_both_unp), s100(k_did_unp)),
                  SE = c(s100se(k_iv_unp), s100se(k_sat_unp), s100se(k_both_unp), s100se(k_did_unp)),
                  `Free time per 100 min` = c(s100(k_iv_ft), s100(k_sat_ft), s100(k_both_ft), s100(k_did_ft)),
                  `SE ` = c(s100se(k_iv_ft), s100se(k_sat_ft), s100se(k_both_ft), s100se(k_did_ft)),
                  `First-stage F` = c(f0(fstat), f1(fstat_sat), f0(fstat_both), f0(fstat_did)), check.names = FALSE)
tab(alt, caption = paste0("Alternative instruments and the falsification-based estimator", syn_note()), label = "alt",
    align = c("l", rep("r", 5)),
    notes = paste0("Regular salaried men 20--59 (last row adds men 20--59 not in paid work, ", fn(nrow(PN) - n_mr), " diaries). Row 1 instruments paid work with Sunday, controlling for Saturday; row 2 with Saturday, controlling for Sunday; row 3 with both (Sargan overidentification p = ", f2(sargan_p), "). Row 4 instruments paid work with Sunday x regular salaried, controlling for Sunday, Saturday, Saturday x regular salaried and status. FSU-clustered SEs."))
```

A Saturday diary changes regular salaried men's paid work by `r est_se(k_fs_sat)`, `r iff(sat_smaller, "less than", "as much as")` a Sunday diary. `r iff(sat_fs_sig, "Saturday is therefore a partial day off for many of these men.", "Saturday is therefore not a reliable shock to paid work in these data.")` Table \ref{tab:alt} compares the allocation implied by each day. `r iff(isTRUE(fstat_sat > 10), paste0("The Saturday instrument implies ", s100x(k_sat_unp), " minutes of unpaid work per 100 forgone, against ", s100(k_iv_unp), " for Sunday."), paste0("The Saturday first stage is weak (F = ", f1(fstat_sat), "), so the Saturday-only estimate is uninformative."))` The Sargan overidentification test of equal allocations has p = `r f2(sargan_p)`; it assumes homoskedastic errors and is indicative only. `r iff(isTRUE(sargan_p > 0.05), "It does not reject, which is consistent with the allocation of released time not depending strongly on which day is released.", "It rejects, which suggests that the use of released time depends on the day, as the synchronisation argument predicts: Sunday is a common holiday for children and other workers, Saturday less so.")`

## Placebo groups and falsification

```{r tab-placebo}
plw <- dcast(PL, group ~ y, value.var = c("est", "se", "p"))
plw <- plw[match(pl_groups, plw$group)]
mk <- function(y_) paste0(f1(plw[[paste0("est_", y_)]]), stars(plw[[paste0("p_", y_)]]), " (", f1(plw[[paste0("se_", y_)]]), ")")
plt <- data.frame(Group = pl_groups, `Paid work` = mk("employment"), `Unpaid work` = mk("unpaid"),
                  `Free time` = mk("free_time"), Learning = mk("learning"),
                  Diaries = fn(PL[y == "employment"][match(pl_groups, group)]$n), check.names = FALSE)
tab(plt, caption = paste0("Sunday effects by usual activity status: men 20--59 (minutes)", syn_note()), label = "placebo",
    align = c("l", rep("r", 5)),
    notes = "Reduced-form coefficients on a Sunday diary (SE in parentheses), with Saturday, controls and fixed effects. Not in paid work: unemployed, attending to domestic duties, or otherwise out of the labour force (excluding students). '--' marks outcomes with no variation in the group. FSU-clustered SEs. * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01.")
```

```{r fig-sun, fig.cap = paste0("Sunday effects by usual activity status, men 20--59", syn_note()), fig.height = 3.6}
PLf <- PL[y %in% c("employment", "unpaid", "free_time") & !is.na(est)]
PLf[, `:=`(yl = factor(pl_y[y], levels = pl_y), gl = factor(group, levels = rev(pl_groups)))]
ggplot(PLf, aes(est, gl)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = est - 1.96 * se, xmax = est + 1.96 * se), colour = SEX_COLS[["Men"]], size = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ yl, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Sunday minus Monday-Friday, minutes per day", y = NULL,
       caption = "Reduced-form coefficients with controls, Saturday indicator and fixed effects. 95% CIs, FSU-clustered.")
```

Table \ref{tab:placebo} and Figure \ref{fig:fig-sun} report the reduced-form Sunday effects for each group of men. The falsification test is the row for men not in paid work. `r iff(is.na(k_nw_emp$est), "They record no paid work on any diary day", paste0("Their paid work changes by ", est_se(k_nw_emp), " on Sundays"))`, and their unpaid work changes by `r est_se(k_nw_unp)`. `r iff(placebo_clean, "The latter is not statistically distinguishable from zero, so there is no evidence of a direct Sunday effect on men's unpaid work that operates outside paid work.", "The latter is statistically significant, which points to a direct effect of the day on men's unpaid work, through the presence of other household members or the weekly rhythm of markets and religion.")` Their free time changes by `r est_se(k_nw_ft)`, `r iff(is_pos(k_nw_ft), "so Sunday raises free time even for men who are not released from work, a sign that the day's social calendar matters for leisure.", "so the free-time response of salaried men is not mirrored among men with nothing to be released from.")`

The school calendar is a channel through which Sunday could change the household's demand for unpaid work. Children aged 6 to 14 who are students spend `r f0(kid_learn_wk)` minutes on learning on an average weekday, and on Sundays they do `r diff_txt(k_kid_learn)` learning. `r iff(is_neg(k_kid_learn), "Children are therefore at home for much of the day on Sundays.", "In these data, the school calendar does not shift children's learning time clearly on Sundays.")` Heterogeneity by the presence of school-age children (below) speaks to whether this matters for fathers' response.

The difference-in-reduced-forms IV in Table \ref{tab:alt} nets out any direct Sunday effect common to salaried men and men not in paid work. It implies `r s100x(k_did_unp)` minutes of unpaid work per 100 forgone, `r iff(did_close, "within the confidence interval of the baseline estimate", "outside the confidence interval of the baseline estimate")`. The identifying assumption is weaker than the exclusion restriction but not innocuous: it requires that the direct Sunday effect on unpaid work be the same for men with and without a salaried job. Men not in paid work are a small and selected group, and the estimate is correspondingly less precise.

```{r fig-sens, fig.cap = paste0("Unpaid-work share under an assumed direct Sunday effect on unpaid work", syn_note()), fig.height = 3}
ggplot(SENS, aes(gamma, 100 * est)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = 100 * (est - 1.96 * se), ymax = 100 * (est + 1.96 * se)), fill = "#9DC3E0", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(colour = SEX_COLS[["Men"]]) +
  { if (isTRUE(is.finite(k_nw_unp$est))) geom_vline(xintercept = k_nw_unp$est, linetype = "dashed", colour = SEX_COLS[["Women"]]) } +
  labs(x = "Assumed direct Sunday effect on unpaid work (minutes)", y = "Unpaid minutes per 100 forgone",
       caption = "IV with outcome = unpaid work minus gamma x Sunday. Band: 95% CI. Dashed line: Sunday effect among men not in paid work.")
```

Figure \ref{fig:fig-sens} shows how the unpaid-work share changes if Sunday raised these men's unpaid work directly by $\gamma$ minutes. `r iff(isTRUE(gamma_zero > 0), paste0("The share falls to zero at a direct effect of ", f1(gamma_zero), " minutes, the full reduced-form effect; any positive direct effect lowers it."), "Because the reduced-form effect on unpaid work is not positive, any positive direct effect makes the implied share negative; the estimate is an upper bound if Sunday raises men's unpaid work directly.")` The dashed line marks the Sunday effect among men not in paid work, a natural benchmark for $\gamma$.

## Heterogeneity

```{r tab-het}
ht <- data.frame(Subgroup = paste0(HET$dim, ": ", HET$level),
                 `First stage (min)` = paste0(f0(HET$fs), " (", f1(HET$fs_se), ")"),
                 `Unpaid per 100 min` = paste0(f1(100 * HET$unp), " (", f1(100 * HET$unp_se), ")"),
                 `Free time per 100 min` = paste0(f1(100 * HET$ft), " (", f1(100 * HET$ft_se), ")"),
                 `p, difference` = f2(HET$pdiff), Diaries = fn(HET$n), check.names = FALSE)
ht$`p, difference`[is.na(HET$pdiff)] <- ""
tab(ht, caption = paste0("Heterogeneity in the allocation of released time: regular salaried men 20--59", syn_note()),
    label = "het", align = c("l", rep("r", 5)),
    notes = "IV estimates within subgroups (SE in parentheses). 'p, difference' tests equality of the unpaid-work share across the two subgroups in a pooled model that interacts paid work, the Sunday instrument, the Saturday control and a subgroup indicator. Wife employed is defined for married men with a linked spouse. FSU-clustered SEs.")
```

Table \ref{tab:het} reports the allocation separately by household and location. Time availability predicts the largest unpaid-work response where the demand for unpaid work is largest, in households with young children. Among regular salaried men with a child under six in the household, the unpaid-work share is `r s100x(hk("Child under 6 in household", "Yes"))` minutes per 100, against `r s100x(hk("Child under 6 in household", "No"))` without. With a school-age child it is `r s100x(hk("Child aged 6--14 in household", "Yes"))`, against `r s100x(hk("Child aged 6--14 in household", "No"))`. In urban areas it is `r s100x(hk("Urban", "Yes"))`, against `r s100x(hk("Urban", "No"))` in rural areas. `r iff("head_grad" %in% names(het_def), paste0("With consumption unavailable, I use the head's education as a socioeconomic proxy: where the household head is a graduate the share is ", s100x(hk("Household head a graduate", "Yes")), ", against ", s100x(hk("Household head a graduate", "No")), " otherwise."), "")` `r iff(length(het_sig) > 0, paste0("The difference is statistically significant at the 5% level for: ", paste(tolower(het_sig), collapse = "; "), "."), "None of these differences is statistically significant at the 5% level; the data do not detect differences in the allocation of released time across these household types and locations, which is not the same as showing that the allocation is the same.")`

## Wives and couples

```{r tab-couple}
ct <- data.frame(Outcome = unname(wy[WT$y]),
                 `Weekday mean` = ifelse(WT$y == "h_share", f2(WT$wk), f0(WT$wk)),
                 `Sunday effect` = paste0(ifelse(WT$y == "h_share", f2(WT$est), f1(WT$est)), stars(WT$p)),
                 SE = ifelse(WT$y == "h_share", f2(WT$se), f1(WT$se)), check.names = FALSE)
tab(ct, caption = paste0("The household's Sunday: wives of regular salaried men and couple outcomes", syn_note()),
    label = "couple", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
    notes = paste0("Couples in which the husband is regular salaried and both diaries refer to the same day (", fn(n_wv), " couples). Reduced-form coefficients on a Sunday diary with Saturday, the wife's controls (including her usual employment status) and fixed effects. Minutes except the husband's share (0 to 1; couples with some unpaid work). The upper bound on joint free time is the smaller of the two spouses' free time; the survey's episode timing would be needed for exact overlap. FSU-clustered SEs. * p<0.10, ** p<0.05, *** p<0.01."))
```

Table \ref{tab:couple} turns to the couple. On the household's Sunday, wives of regular salaried men do `r diff_txt(k_w_unp)` unpaid work, `r diff_txt(k_w_ft)` free time and `r diff_txt(k_w_emp)` paid work than on a weekday. `r iff(wives_down, "Wives' unpaid work falls, so some of the husband's unpaid work substitutes for hers.", iff(wives_up, "Wives' unpaid work rises, so the household's demand for unpaid work rises on Sundays by more than the husband takes on.", "Wives' unpaid work does not change detectably, so the husband's day off does not relieve the wife of unpaid work."))` Scaled by the husband's first stage, the wife's unpaid work changes by `r s100x(k_w_iv)` minutes per 100 minutes of the husband's paid work forgone, and the couple's total unpaid work by `r s100x(k_c_iv)`.

The wife-minus-husband gap in unpaid work, `r f0(gap_wk)` minutes on an average weekday, is `r diff_txt(k_gap, "larger", "smaller")` on Sundays. The husband's share of the couple's unpaid work, `r f2(hsh_wk)` on weekdays, is `r diff_pp(k_hsh)` on Sundays. `r iff(gap_down, "The division of unpaid work is more equal on Sundays, although the gap remains large.", "The division of unpaid work is not detectably more equal on Sundays.")`

Joint free time is the time both spouses are free at once. Without the timing of each spouse's episodes, I bound it from above by the smaller of the two spouses' free time. On weekdays this upper bound is `r f0(jf_wk)` minutes, and it changes by `r est_se(k_jf)` on Sundays. `r iff(is_pos(k_jf), "The household's Sunday raises the free time spouses can spend together, consistent with the value of synchronised leisure [@hamermesh2002timing; @jenkins2005nobody].", "The household's Sunday does not detectably raise the free time spouses could spend together.")`

The wife's response mixes the husband's day off with the household's Sunday: her own working day, the children's school day and the weekly calendar also change. Comparing wives of salaried men with wives of men not in paid work isolates the part due to the husband's day off. The difference in their Sunday effects on unpaid work is `r est_se(k_wdid_unp)`, and on free time `r est_se(k_wdid_ft)`. `r iff(is_sig(k_wdid_unp), "The husband's day off itself thus changes the wife's unpaid work.", "The husband's day off itself does not detectably change the wife's unpaid work beyond the household's Sunday.")`

## Robustness

```{r tab-rob}
rt <- data.frame(Specification = ROB$spec, `First stage` = paste0(f0(ROB$fs), " (", f1(ROB$fs_se), ")"),
                 F = f0(ROB$F), `Unpaid per 100 min` = paste0(f1(100 * ROB$unp), " (", f1(100 * ROB$unp_se), ")"),
                 `Free time per 100 min` = paste0(f1(100 * ROB$ft), " (", f1(100 * ROB$ft_se), ")"),
                 N = fn(ROB$n), check.names = FALSE)
tab(rt, caption = paste0("Robustness of the allocation estimates: regular salaried men 20--59", syn_note()),
    label = "rob", align = c("l", rep("r", 5)),
    notes = paste0("IV estimates (SE in parentheses) of minutes of unpaid work and free time per 100 minutes of paid work forgone, instrumented by a Sunday diary. Baseline: ", fe_txt, " fixed effects. FSU fixed effects compare diaries within the same village or urban block; FSUs with a single diary drop out. Normal days only keeps diaries the respondent described as a normal day. FSU-clustered SEs."))
```

Table \ref{tab:rob} varies the specification. The checks drop all controls, which should matter little under random assignment; replace district fixed effects with coarser state fixed effects, with district-by-sub-round fixed effects, which compare households in the same district and quarter, or with FSU fixed effects, which compare households in the same village or urban block interviewed on different days and absorb local differences in interview schedules; control for proxy reporting or keep only self-reported diaries, because diaries reported by another household member may understate men's unpaid work [@lee2005husbands]; drop Saturday diaries, so that Sunday is compared only with Monday to Friday; restrict to married men; `r iff(has_td, "keep only diaries that the respondent described as a normal day, which removes festivals, illness and other unusual days (and possibly some weekly days off); ", "")`and drop the survey weights [@solon2015weighting]. Across the `r nrow(ROB)` specifications the unpaid-work share ranges from `r f1(100 * rob_range[1])` to `r f1(100 * rob_range[2])` minutes per 100. `r iff(rob_stable, "Every estimate lies within the 95% confidence interval of the baseline, so the conclusions do not depend on these choices.", "At least one estimate lies outside the 95% confidence interval of the baseline, so the conclusions are sensitive to specification and the baseline should be read with that in mind.")`

# Discussion {#sec:discussion}

## What the Sunday estimate measures

The estimate is the share of a forgone paid-work minute that regular salaried men allocate to unpaid work on their weekly day off. Three features of the experiment shape how it generalises.

First, the day off is anticipated and recurs. Weekly tasks such as shopping, repairs and dealing with officials can be moved to it, which would make the unpaid-work share larger on Sundays than under a permanent reduction spread over the week. `r iff(isTRUE(male_share > core_share), "The task breakdown fits this: much of the response is in shopping, repairs and household management, which are easily batched.", "The task breakdown does not suggest that batching dominates: the response is not concentrated in shopping, repairs and household management.")` Daily tasks such as cooking and cleaning cannot be postponed in the same way, so the Sunday response in these tasks is a closer guide to what a shorter working day would do.

Second, Sunday synchronises the household. Children are out of school, many wives who work are off, and friends and relatives are free. This raises the value of leisure on Sundays relative to a day off taken alone, and it also changes the amount of unpaid work to be done. The Saturday comparison and the heterogeneity by children speak to this. A reform that shortened every working day, rather than lengthening the weekend, would release time when the rest of the household is not at home. On these grounds it might move more of the released time into unpaid work.

Third, the estimate is local to compliers, regular salaried men who work on weekdays and not on Sundays. Regular salaried employment accounts for `r pct(share_reg)` of employed men aged 20 to 59 in the sample. The response of casual and self-employed men to a reduction in working time could differ, and the design does not identify their response because Sunday is a less predictable shock to their paid work.

## Measurement

Diaries reported by another household member may understate men's unpaid work [@lee2005husbands], and Sunday diaries are `r diff_pp(k_proxy_sun, "more", "less")` likely to be proxy-reported. `r iff(has(MR, "proxy_report"), paste0("With proxy reporting controlled for, the unpaid-work share is ", f1(100 * ROB[spec == "Adds proxy-report indicator"]$unp), " minutes per 100, and among self-reported diaries it is ", f1(100 * ROB[spec == "Self-reported diaries only"]$unp), ", against ", s100(k_iv_unp), " in the baseline."), "")` The TUS records the main activity in each half-hour slot and, separately, simultaneous activities. A man who minds children while watching television is recorded as doing one of the two as the major activity. If such passive care rises on Sundays and is recorded as leisure, the unpaid-work share understates men's involvement. Secondary activities could be used to bound this.

## Implications for policy

`r iff(pass, "A substantial fraction of the time released from paid work goes into unpaid work. Shorter working hours for salaried men would, on this evidence, shift some unpaid work towards them.", "Only a small fraction of the time released from paid work goes into unpaid work. On this evidence, shorter working hours alone would do little to change the gender division of unpaid work.")` The comparison with paternity leave is instructive. Leave policies that reserve time for fathers combine released time with an explicit expectation of care, and some of them have lasting effects on fathers' involvement [@patnaik2019reserving; @tamm2019fathers], while others do not [@ekberg2013parental]. A day off provides time without the expectation. If men use it mostly for rest, the binding constraint on their unpaid work is not time, and policies that work on expectations, through leave reserved for fathers, school and childcare schedules, or information about other men's behaviour [@bursztyn2020misperceived], are more promising than policies that only shorten hours. The wife's response matters as much as the husband's: `r iff(gap_down, "the narrowing of the within-couple gap on Sundays shows that some of the husband's additional unpaid work relieves the wife.", "the absence of a detectable narrowing of the within-couple gap on Sundays shows that the husband's day off does not relieve the wife.")`

## Limitations

The exclusion restriction cannot be proven. The falsification test and the difference-in-reduced-forms estimator address the most obvious direct channels, but they rely on men not in paid work being comparable to salaried men in how Sunday affects their unpaid work, and these men are a small, selected group. The diary covers a single day per person, so the comparison is across people interviewed on different days, not within a person's week [@frazis2012think]. Wives' time use is observed on the same day as the husband's, but the measure of joint free time is an upper bound, because the analysis panel holds daily totals rather than the timing of episodes. The survey does not record whether a respondent's employer gives Sunday off, so the first stage is estimated rather than known. Finally, the person-level file lacks the household questionnaire, so religion, caste, consumption expenditure, cooking fuel, the mode of laundry and sweeping, special-care needs, land and dwelling are unavailable. I cannot control for them, test balance on them or study heterogeneity by them; district and sub-round fixed effects and the roster-based socioeconomic proxies absorb some, but not all, of this variation, and balance on these unobserved characteristics is assumed rather than shown.

# Conclusion {#sec:conclusion}

The weekly day off is a recurring experiment in men's time. India's Time Use Survey 2024 records the day before the interview for households interviewed across the week, which turns it into a shock to regular salaried men's paid work that `r iff(bal_ok, "is balanced on observed pre-determined characteristics within district and quarter", "is only partly balanced on observed pre-determined characteristics, so the estimates condition on them")`. `r iff(sig_unp, paste0("These men allocate ", s100(k_iv_unp), " of every 100 minutes released from paid work to unpaid domestic and care work, a statistically significant share,"), paste0("These men allocate ", s100(k_iv_unp), " of every 100 minutes released from paid work to unpaid domestic and care work, a share not statistically distinguishable from zero,"))` and `r s100(k_iv_ft)` to free time and `r s100(k_iv_sl)` to sleep. `r iff(gap_down, "Their wives' unpaid work responds enough that the within-couple gap narrows on Sundays.", "The within-couple gap in unpaid work does not narrow detectably on Sundays.")` `r iff(pass, "Time availability is a real constraint on men's unpaid work, and working-time policy can be part of a strategy for a more equal division.", "Time availability is not the main constraint on men's unpaid work, and working-time policy alone is unlikely to change the division of unpaid work in India.")` The same design is available in any time-use survey that records "yesterday" and spreads interviews across the week, and applying it elsewhere would show whether this conclusion is specific to India.
